scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Marinera Norteña traces its roots to the ancient Mochic dance and was influenced by Spanish contradanza and Andean zamacueca.
The dance was renamed 'Marinera' in 1879 by Abelardo Gamarra to honor the Peruvian Navy during the War of the Pacific.
Trujillo has been recognized as the national birthplace of the Marinera since 1986.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Marinera Norteña is performed at cultural festivals, notably the National Festival of the Marinera in Trujillo, and at competitions held since 1960.
It symbolizes courtship and cultural identity of northern Peru.
The dance honors historical events like the War of the Pacific and celebrates Peru's mestizo heritage.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Marinera Norteña is danced by a male and female partner who use handkerchiefs to flirt and court.
Women dance barefoot, moving gracefully yet swiftly, often on hot or rough surfaces, while men wear shoes and traditional attire.
The dance features quick footwork, zapateo (foot stomping) by men, and coquettish gestures by women.
Watch for Zapateo, Barefoot Flick, Handkerchief Wave.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music accompanying Marinera Norteña includes cajón, clarinets, guitars, drums, and bugles, played in a four-beat rhythm.
The sound is lively and rhythmic, combining Afro-Peruvian percussion with Spanish melodic instruments.
Listen for the cajón, clarinet, guitar, drums.
The pulse is 4/4.
The music combines the percussive pulse of the cajón with melodic clarinet and guitar, creating a rhythmic, bright, and engaging sound that drives the quick-paced dance.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Men typically wear 'chalan' clothing: cotton ponchos or suits with wide straw hats and black glossy shoes.
Women wear ample white skirts adorned with lace and dance barefoot, a tradition rooted in 19th-century rural northern Peru.
The dance is often performed outdoors on pavements, sometimes at noon when the ground is hottest, showcasing women's endurance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Abelardo Gamarra, known as 'El Tunante', renamed the dance 'Marinera' in 1879.
Augusto Áscuez Villanueva (1892-1985) is recognized as a principal interpreter.
Marinera Norteña is one of three main Marinera variants, alongside Marinera Limeña (from Lima, slower and more elegant) and Marinera Serrana (from the highlands, slower and more sentimental).
Marinera Norteña descends from the ancient Mochic dance, influenced by Spanish contradanza and Andean zamacueca.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Marinera Norteña is regional variant of Marinera Limeña: Slower, more elegant coastal variant from Lima with footwear for women.
Marinera Norteña is regional variant of Marinera Serrana: Highland variant with slower tempo and sentimental style.
Marinera Norteña is ancestor of Zamacueca: Precursor dance from which Marinera evolved.
Marinera Norteña is related of Cueca: Chilean dance sharing common roots with Marinera.
